items.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Detecting Satirical Code-Mixed Sentences
items.abstract: Code-switching is a natural linguistic phenomenon, yet its impact on high-level reasoning tasks remains largely unexplored in under-resourced languages like Romanian. Natural language processing tasks, such as satire detection, rely heavily on nuanced cultural and syntactic cues that large language models struggle to capture. In this paper, we investigate four methods (i.e., random replacement, phrase translation, dependency parsing, and large language models) for generating synthetic code-mixed Romanian sentences with English, German, French, and Italian. We start with an existing dataset for satire detection, compiled from Romanian news articles and annotated at the sentence level by humans, and augment it with over 600k samples, namely CS-SeLeRoSa. We provide an in-depth analysis of the dataset generation process. Then, we evaluate several multilingual large language models across zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and fine-tuning regimes on both the synthetic corpus and a human-adjudicated gold benchmark, namely CS-SeLeRoSa-Gold. While older open models suffer substantial degradation (dropping to 37%-55% macro-F1), newer models like Gemma 4 31B achieve 68.1% zero-shot, rivaling frontier models like GPT-5 mini (69.5%). Furthermore, fine-tuning significantly reduces formatting errors and improves the results, increasing Gemma 4 31B to 77.5% on CS-SeLeRoSa and 72.6% on the gold standard, outperforming frontier zero-shot baselines.

items.title: Benefits of Autoethnography Across the Teaching Career Span: An Argument for Inclusion
items.abstract: Abstract Developing the capacity for self-reflection is a central component of continual teacher growth. Practices such as journaling help educators rapidly improve by enabling them to identify challenges in lesson planning, assessment, behavior management, and classroom culture. Autoethnography, a research method that integrates reflective journal entries with existing scholarship, offers a structured approach for deepening this self-reflective work. Introducing autoethnographic practices to both future and current educators can therefore cultivate stronger reflective habits across all stages of a teaching career. For preservice teachers, engaging in autoethnography encourages them to connect their emerging classroom observations with established research, promoting evidence-based decision-making early in their professional development. These reflective habits can support long-term success by helping new teachers internalize practices that foster continuous improvement. For teachers in their first years, autoethnography provides a tool for managing the steep learning curve they face as they encounter educational challenges for the first time. Reflective journaling paired with research can offer clarity, reduce overwhelm, and help them make sense of their experiences. Veteran teachers also benefit from autoethnographic practices, as the method can deepen their understanding of complex or evolving issues—such as the growing influence of artificial intelligence in classrooms—by linking ongoing experiences with contemporary scholarship. Finally, teacher educators who use autoethnography themselves gain methodological proficiency, strengthen their own teaching, and develop authentic examples to share with those they mentor. This chapter explores the value of integrating autoethnographic practices into teacher education to support reflective growth at all career stages.

items.title: Between automation and epistemic autonomy: reappropriating generative AI in global academic writing
items.abstract: This article examines the epistemic implications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in academic writing within unequal knowledge infrastructures. I conceptualize it as an epistemic apparatus: a sociotechnical arrangement that mediates credibility, voice, and scholarly legitimacy. Drawing on epistemic injustice theory, post- and decolonial scholarship, and critical AI studies, the article argues that GenAI can reinforce dominant Anglophone norms of academic form, reshaping the conditions under which knowledge becomes legible and publishable. I argue that these effects emerge through interactions among models, writing practices, and institutional expectations. Through two author-constructed fictional analytic vignettes, the article illustrates how selective uptake, compromise, diagnostic testing, and refusal can operate as practices of judgment within AI-mediated writing. I conceptualize epistemic autonomy as situated authority over scholarly judgment and advance critical epistemic literacy as a pedagogical orientation for exercising that authority under algorithmic mediation. The article concludes by proposing an epistemic ethics of governance oriented toward traceability, plurality, infrastructural accountability, and the protection of bounded use and refusal.

items.title: Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics
items.abstract: Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment. To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive 84-label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets: DiagBase, which covers single- and multi-turn prompts with direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks, and DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations -- substantially higher than the 69%-87% achieved by the baselines -- and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.864). Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi-turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.

items.title: Beyond capability frameworks: Australia’s next challenge in preparing the digital health workforce
items.abstract: Australia has made substantial progress in digital health workforce development through the establishment of nationally coordinated strategies, profession-specific capability frameworks, and the Australian Digital Health Capability Framework. Collectively, these initiatives have repositioned digital health from a specialised technical domain to a core professional competency expected across the health workforce. However, while considerable effort has focused on defining the capabilities required for contemporary digital practice, less attention has been directed towards ensuring workforce readiness. This perspective argues that capability and readiness are related but distinct concepts. Capability frameworks describe the knowledge, skills, and behaviours expected of health professionals, whereas readiness reflects the ability to apply these capabilities confidently, ethically, and adaptively within rapidly evolving healthcare environments. As digital health systems become increasingly influenced by artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and data-driven decision-making, workforce preparedness will depend on more than technical competence alone. It will require critical thinking, ethical reasoning, digital and data literacies, and the capacity to work effectively alongside emerging technologies. We propose that, while capability frameworks will continue to evolve alongside technological and regulatory change, Australia's next challenge is ensuring that existing capability expectations are translated into educational practice, workplace learning, professional development, and measurable workforce outcomes. Sustained implementation, evaluation, and collaboration will be essential to ensure a future-ready digital health workforce.

items.title: Beyond End-to-End Recovery: Towards a Better Understanding of LLM Steganography via Rolewise Decomposition
items.abstract: In large language model (LLM) steganography, an encoder hides a private message in an otherwise ordinary response, as text transmitted to a decoder, who attempts to recover it. The success of this private-message transmission is commonly measured through end-to-end (E2E) recovery, which checks whether the decoder correctly reconstructs the private message. However, E2E recovery cannot distinguish encoding failures from decoding failures or reveal how the private message is represented in the encoder's transmitted text. To address these limitations, we introduce a rolewise decomposition framework that separately examines how private messages are represented in encoder transmitted texts, what decoders recover, and what deterministic verification can establish. Across 7,200 encoder responses, we identify 168 verifiable encodings missed by decoders and 706 responses containing private messages reconstructed through word-length or token-initial patterns not explicitly specified in the encoder's instructions. These findings demonstrate that E2E recovery alone may obscure important distinctions between encoding and decoding, motivating their separate evaluation to better understand and mitigate the safety issues caused by LLM steganography.

items.title: Beyond novice-to-expert progression: a context-enabled continuing professional development framework derived from nursing practice in resource-constrained South African hospitals
items.abstract: Continuing professional development (CPD) is frequently organised as a sequence of educational events directed at individual practitioners. In resource-constrained health services, however, participation and learning transfer are shaped by staffing, protected time, leadership, finance, infrastructure, access to current guidance and opportunities to apply learning. Individual-centred and linear developmental models do not adequately explain these interactions. This article proposes the Context-Enabled Continuing Professional Development (CE-CPD) Framework, derived from a programme of research involving a scoping review, qualitative evidence from professional nurses and nurse managers in Limpopo Province, South Africa, and critical engagement with developmental, implementation and CPD-outcomes literature. The framework positions professional learning within four interacting layers: a stakeholder and service ecosystem, organisational enabling conditions, a recurring five-phase workplace learning cycle, and an outcome pathway extending from access and participation to practitioner capability, professional behaviour, team and organisational performance, and patient or population health. Capability development is treated as domain-specific, iterative and potentially non-linear, rather than as an automatic progression from novice to expert. Six propositions specify how contextual readiness, protected opportunity, equitable access, workplace application, knowledge sharing and infrastructure are expected to influence these outcomes. The CE-CPD Framework shifts the explanatory focus from whether professionals attend CPD to whether their organisations make relevant learning possible and ensure its sustainable application. Although derived from nursing evidence, its organisational mechanisms may be relevant across healthcare professions. Interprofessional co-design, prospective testing and equity-sensitive evaluation are required before wider adoption.

items.title: Beyond Predictive Accuracy: A CPST Perspective on Systemic Bottlenecks and Reconnection Pathways for Environmental AI
items.abstract: Environmental artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly improving prediction across Earth system forecasting, remote sensing, and biodiversity monitoring, yet predictive skill out paces scientific understanding, data and models remain fragmented across environmental and human-system contexts, and the capacity to govern and act on AI is unevenly distributed. Using the Cyber-Physical-Social-Thinking (CPST) framework, we locate these gaps in relations rather than in individual models: a prediction-understanding rupture (weak Cyber-Thinking coupling), cross-domain fragmentation (incomplete Cyber-Physical-Social integration), and a science-governance-equity gap (weak Thinking-Social coupling with asymmetric Cyber-Social capacity). We specify semantic, procedural, and institutional dimensions along which these relations fail, and propose that the three bottlenecks are mutually reinforcing. Set against knowledge-systems research on credibility, salience, and legitimacy, the CPST lens adds one distinction: it separates the inference performed by a model from the scientific interpretation of its outputs, so that evidential warrant and institutional authority can fail independently. Three reconnection pathways follow, namely epistemically anchored environmental AI, interoperable environmental AI systems, and participatory environmental-AI governance, each with evaluation criteria that extend beyond predictive accuracy. Applied to operational flood forecasting, the diagnosis yields a procedure that identifies the binding relation, predicts where the limiting factor moves once that relation is strengthened, and states the evidence that would disconfirm the ranking. Progress should be judged by whether digital capability remains connected to physical processes, scientific reasoning, and societal institutions in ways that are reliable, interpretable, and fit for purpose.

items.title: Beyond Predictive Performance: An Explainability–Governance Score Framework for Multidimensional Machine Learning Model Selection
items.abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision systems where predictive performance alone may provide an insufficient basis for responsible model selection. Although explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) offers techniques for interpreting model behavior, existing evaluation approaches often assess explanation properties independently and provide limited support for integrated model selection. This study proposes the Explainability–Governance Score (EGS) Framework, a multidimensional decision-support methodology integrating four complementary dimensions: Fidelity, local predictive Stability, Counterfactual Actionability, and Governance Alignment. The framework combines established XAI techniques, practical recourse, and governance-oriented criteria into a composite evaluation of candidate models. It is empirically evaluated using five machine learning models across three high-stakes domains represented by the German Credit, Pima Indians Diabetes, and COMPAS datasets. Under the primary BPS specification, predictive evaluation ranked XGBoost, Decision Tree, and Random Forest highest in Credit Risk, Healthcare, and Criminal Justice, respectively. Under the multidimensional EGS evaluation, Logistic Regression achieved the highest EGS in Credit Risk (0.915) and Healthcare (0.915), while Decision Tree achieved the highest EGS in Criminal Justice (0.886). The identity of the highest-EGS model remained unchanged across all six prespecified weighting configurations in each domain. These findings demonstrate that multidimensional EGS evaluation can materially influence candidate-model rankings relative to predictive evaluation and provide a structured, reproducible basis for evaluating candidate models beyond predictive performance alone.

items.title: Beyond Property Management: A Systems Engineering Approach to Scalable PropTech Solutions
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of Property Technology (PropTech) has fundamentally transformed the role of software within the real estate industry. Early PropTech solutions primarily focused on digitizing isolated operational activities such as leasing, maintenance management, accounting, and customer communication. As digital ecosystems have matured, however, the engineering challenge has shifted from developing individual applications to designing complex systems capable of integrating physical infrastructure, enterprise software, cloud services, artificial intelligence, Internet of Things (IoT), and human decision-making into unified operational environments. This article argues that future PropTech platforms should be understood not merely as software products but as large-scale systems whose behavior emerges from the interaction of numerous interconnected technical and organizational components. Adopting a systems engineering perspective enables organizations to address scalability, interoperability, resilience, lifecycle management, stakeholder coordination, and long-term system evolution more effectively than traditional software-centric approaches. The article introduces a systems engineering framework specifically designed for scalable PropTech ecosystems, integrating principles of system decomposition, requirements engineering, operational resilience, lifecycle management, human-system collaboration, and continuous architectural evolution. Rather than emphasizing individual technologies, the proposed framework focuses on engineering digital real estate ecosystems that remain adaptable, reliable, and sustainable throughout decades of operational change. Contemporary platform-based engineering research likewise emphasizes adaptability and long-term evolvability as essential characteristics of complex digital systems.

items.title: Beyond Small Talk: Modeling Disclosure Trajectories in Human-AI Conversation
items.abstract: Recently, we see a rise in conversational agents as a form of social and emotional support, where disclosure will unfold over time. Yet, current evaluations of these agents typically examine isolated conversational states. In analyses of naturally occurring conversations, disclosure history and current disclosure are confounded which tends to make their effects difficult to isolate. We thus introduce Trajectory-based Disclosure Evaluation (TraDE), an evaluation framework grounded in Social Penetration Theory that utilizes predefined disclosure trajectories and evaluates how preceding disclosure history shapes model behavior under matched current disclosure. Through the use of TraDE, we demonstrate across multiple models and relational behavior benchmarks that responses to disclosures matched on depth can differ depending on the preceding trajectory, particularly in whether models accept or challenge the user's framing. We also observed that these differences track accumulated exposure to deeper disclosure rather than any single moment of vulnerability or the order of disclosures. It also tends to persists for several turns after disclosure returns to shallow levels. For several behaviors, we also demonstrate that models diverge most consistently from human supporters in the Emotional Support Conversation corpus (ESConv) not when users open up but rather when they step back in their disclosure. TraDE thus provides a systematic way to expose history-dependent relational behavior that evaluations of isolated conversational states would otherwise miss.

items.title: Beyond the Algorithm: Integrating AI into Applied Learning Pedagogy—A Critical Inquiry
items.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen applied learning in the social sciences by transforming raw information into analyzable material that students actively interpret, evaluate, and convert into disciplinary knowledge. It argues that AI, when guided by theoretical rigor and ethical awareness, enhances critical pedagogy by supporting qualitative interpretation, computational analysis, simulation based inquiry, and independent reasoning. Rather than replacing instruction, AI functions as an analytical scaffold that students interrogate, correct, and contextualize, enabling deeper engagement with social structures, patterned behavior, and institutional dynamics.

items.title: Beyond the Human Negotiator: Generative AI and the Threshold of Autonomous Decision‐Making
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in negotiation, evaluating contemporary systems through the specific case study of Large Language Models (LLMs). To address the lack of established terminology, it first proposes a new typology distinguishing Negotiation Supported by AI (NSAI), Negotiation by Controlled AI (NCAI), and Negotiation by Autonomous AI (NAAI). To determine whether current systems can achieve genuine NAAI, the article first develops the Core Essential Elements of Negotiation (CEEN) through a structured comparison of authoritative definitions of negotiation and then examines how these literature‐derived elements align with the perceptions of 250 survey respondents. Finally, the paper applies an ordered analytical rule to contemporary LLMs. Information Exchange and Reciprocity are directly instantiable; Outcome, Divergent Motivations, and Interdependence are externally conditioned; and Choice is not currently instantiable because an attributable evaluative standpoint and consequential commitment remain absent. Accordingly, current LLM‐based negotiating systems remain controlled rather than autonomous agents under the proposed typology.

items.title: Beyond the Vote: When Do LLMs Add Value to Retrieval-Based Tabular Classification?
items.abstract: Retrieval-based in-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict tabular labels from similar examples, but it remains unclear whether LLM inference improves on direct voting over those same examples. We address this question by comparing four general-purpose LLMs with distance-weighted nearest-neighbor voting (Distance-KNN) using identical retrieved neighbors across 19 tabular classification datasets. With the number of demonstrations fixed, enlarging the retrieval candidate pool improves accuracy for all predictors, yet Distance-KNN achieves the highest mean accuracy at every pool size. More detailed analyses reveal that LLM gains are concentrated where retrieved neighbors exhibit low label consensus and vary across models. These gains further depend on the average feature-space distance to the test query: under low label consensus, some LLMs outperform Distance-KNN in close and intermediate neighborhoods, but all fall behind on average in the most distant group. Complementary experiments on the number of demonstrations, prompt formulation, retrieval representation, and label-balanced demonstration selection largely preserve the overall findings. These results characterize when LLM inference adds predictive value beyond distance-weighted voting in retrieval-based tabular ICL.

items.title: Bottom‐up and top‐down problem solving with agentic AI
items.abstract: Abstract Agentic LLM agents can sometimes seem like magic, granting our (almost) every wish. But like the magic genies in stories like the Sorcerer's Apprentice, sometimes you have to be careful what you wish for. The difficulty of precisely specifying what it is we want and unintended consequences, sometimes derail this magic. As with genies, they grant requests in a top‐down manner. The agent autonomously breaks the wish into subgoals, until it reaches concrete actions that can be done by Agentic facilities. If left unsupervised by the user, a misunderstanding can result in disaster. But it's also possible to adopt a bottom‐up approach, starting with concrete examples, demonstrating procedures on these examples, and only then generalizing to a wider set of cases. It is often easier to control and debug, and easier for beginners and nontechnical people. Ultimately, we need flexibility to go in either direction. The contribution of this paper is to bring a bottom‐up methodology to “vibe coding” with Agentic Agents like Cowork and ChatGPT Agent. It draws on the technique of Programming by Example (also called Programming by Demonstration) for conventional programming. The advent of Agentic AI may unblock a 50‐year obstacle that has prevented PBE from more widespread acceptance.

items.title: Boundary Project: Unified Continuity Science and Recoverability-Constrained Systems — Expanded Meta-Universal Living-System Edition
items.abstract: This publication presents a consolidated archival and computational release of the Boundary Project, developed within the Continuity Science and Recoverability-Constrained Systems research programme. The corpus brings together mathematical formulations of recoverability, admissible successor spaces, irreversible transitions, protected continuity, operational distinction, recursive governance, system evolution, evidence provenance, institutional accountability, and the preservation of future possibilities. Its central research proposition is that material transitions should be evaluated not only according to present-state validity, immediate performance, or predicted outcomes, but also according to the recoverable future states that remain reachable following execution. The finite successor-space formalism represents operational systems through distinguishable states, transitions, admissibility relations, protected correspondence, and temporal execution constraints. For a state X, the admissibly reachable successor structure C*(X) represents the future-state structure reachable through admissible continuation. Relative to a protected target class G, recoverability is expressed as: R(X,G) = 1 if and only if C(X) intersects G.* This formulation distinguishes operational continuation from recoverable continuation. A system may remain operational while progressively losing independent correction paths, recovery options, supporting reserves, or the ability to preserve protected correspondence. The associated mathematical research examines reachability, fixed points, invariant kernels, closure operators, transition algebra, bisimulation, recoverability topology, possibility collapse, uncertainty, resource dependence, timing constraints, and finite-state verification. The broader programme develops these principles into technical, institutional, legal, biological, ecological, financial, computational, and human-centred architectures. Unified conceptual architecture The corpus is organized around a common operational grammar connecting distinguishable entities, states, events, relations, intervals, boundaries, dependencies, transitions, effects, outcomes, and successor possibilities. It treats recoverability as a property of actual executable continuation under the relevant conditions, rather than merely the theoretical existence of a possible corrective action. Core architectural elements include: Distinction and operational representation Protected identity and correspondence Authority, consent, and admissibility State and transition modelling Finite successor-space reachability Recovery intervals and temporal constraints Independent correction and restoration paths Evidence provenance and traceability Recursive governance and institutional accountability Future possibility preservation Controlled succession and re-entry Self-referential evaluation of recovery and governance mechanisms These elements are applied across interconnected domains rather than treated as unrelated research proposals. Zero-Distinction Boundary The Zero-Distinction Boundary is the formal and epistemic limit of operational specification. Any model capable of evaluating states, comparing outcomes, recognizing identities, establishing relations, testing evidence, or preserving recoverability must distinguish something. When no additional operational distinction can be expressed without reintroducing distinction itself, the formal reduction reaches its expression boundary. This condition does not establish metaphysical nothingness, the ultimate physical nature of reality, or universal scientific completeness. It identifies the point at which the current formal system cannot generate a further meaningful operational distinction. A subsequently discovered material distinction may reopen the analysis. Meta-universal and recursive architecture The consolidated programme extends its governing principles to higher-order structures, including systems of systems, federated architectures, nested governance, adaptive frameworks, distributed representations, cross-domain dependencies, and evolving successor organizations. The meta-level framework treats the rules, evaluators, models, interfaces, verification processes, recovery resources, and governance mechanisms themselves as operational objects subject to examination. The intention is to prevent architectural changes, administrative classifications, technological substitutions, or recursive delegation from silently defeating the original recoverability requirements. The nine-dimensional expansion framework provides a finite combinatorial organization for exploring distinctions across orientation, time, roles, protected values, failures, responses, scope, evidence, and governance. Its combinatorial search space supports structured exploration and generation of test cases. It does not establish that every configuration is physically possible, scientifically novel, or empirically validated. Technical and computational applications The corpus includes material relating to processor-implemented operational determination, recoverability-constrained authorization, software and hardware continuity, input-output provenance, communication systems, distributed machine coordination, industrial transition isolation, artificial intelligence governance, financial continuity, healthcare systems engineering, water security, ecological systems, and other cross-domain research architectures. These applications share the principle of testing whether a proposed action preserves the necessary conditions for timely correction, restoration, substitution, containment, or admissible continuation. Where recoverability cannot be established, the proposed frameworks favour preserving a less irreversible state while additional evidence, authority, or corrective capacity is established. Legal, constitutional, and institutional dimensions The associated constitutional and governance materials propose principles concerning truthful distinction, human dignity, informed consent, legitimate authority, institutional responsibility, evidence preservation, accountable succession, restoration, and prevention of avoidable irreversible harm. These texts are proposed models for adoption and evaluation. Publication does not itself create binding national law, international treaty obligations, regulatory certification, or institutional adoption. Software and executable components The consolidated release preserves software-related material and research implementations associated with local corpus indexing, data integrity, evidence management, finite-state reachability, mathematical evaluation, and recoverability-oriented decision support. Individual implementations vary in completeness and validation status. Inclusion in this archive does not mean that every described architecture has been converted into a production-ready application or independently certified for safety-critical deployment. Archival construction and preservation This edition consists of nine ZIP volumes that preserve fifteen source archives from earlier Boundary consolidation and reconstruction releases. The preservation procedure retains historical versions and uses SHA-256 integrity verification to establish byte-level correspondence between the preserved source archives and their restored copies. An earlier damaged archive was also subjected to partial file-level recovery, with successfully recovered entries separated from unresolved source material. The present edition retains both earlier six-part releases and supplementary material rather than assuming that independently reconstructed archives are automatically complete substitutes for original source data. Verification and completeness boundaries This publication distinguishes four different forms of completeness: Archival integrity: verification that preserved source bytes match the corresponding recorded hashes. Finite formal completeness: exhaustive evaluation within explicitly defined finite states, transitions, constraints, and protected target classes. Implementation completeness: the extent to which specified functions have been implemented and successfully tested. Empirical completeness: the extent to which the model and its assumptions have been independently validated against actual operating conditions. Byte-level archival verification does not by itself prove semantic equivalence, operational correctness, scientific novelty, universal applicability, or completeness across all possible future systems. Real-world scientific, engineering, legal, and institutional applications require independent validation appropriate to their respective domains. Research significance The Boundary Project proposes a common language for examining how systems change while preserving materially necessary truth, identity, agency, responsibility, evidence, correction capacity, and recoverable future possibility. Its contribution as a research programme lies in bringing mathematical successor-state reasoning, temporal recoverability, technical control, institutional governance, and cross-domain continuity into one interoperable conceptual and computational framework. The programme invites formal analysis, independent replication, practical implementation, adversarial testing, domain-specific refinement, and comparative evaluation against existing methods in control theory, resilience engineering, safety, law, governance, and complex-systems research. Preservation and citation This Zenodo record should be cited as the consolidated nine-part preservation edition of the Boundary Project. Researchers should cite individual source publications or patent filings when referring to a specific theorem, technical disclosure, experiment, or legal instrument contained in the archive. items.title: Brain Tumour Detection Using EfficientNet-Transformer Hybrid Network with SHAP and Grad-CAM Based Explainable Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Accurate and interpretable brain tumour detection from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains a significant challenge in computer-aided diagnosis. This study proposes an EfficientNet–Transformer Hybrid Network integrated with SHapley Additive ExPlanations (SHAP) and Grad-CAM explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques for automated and trustworthy brain tumour classification. Methods: The proposed framework combines EfficientNet for local feature extraction and a Vision Transformer for global contextual learning. MRI images from publicly available benchmark datasets containing four classes (glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumour, and no tumour) were preprocessed and augmented before training. The model was trained using an 80:20 training-testing split, while SHAP and Grad-CAM were employed to provide feature-level and spatial explanations of predictions. Results: The proposed framework achieved a classification accuracy of 98.88%, outperforming several state-of-the-art CNN and transformer models. It also attained average precision, recall, and F1-score values of 98.90%, 98.88%, and 98.89%, respectively, with an average AUC of 0.9893. Ablation and robustness analyses demonstrated that integrating SHAP and Grad-CAM improved interpretability while maintaining high predictive performance under noisy conditions. Conclusions: The proposed EfficientNet–Transformer framework effectively combines local and global feature learning with dual explainability mechanisms to deliver accurate and clinically interpretable brain tumour classification. The results demonstrate its potential as a reliable computer-aided diagnosis tool for neuro-oncology and clinical decision support systems.

items.title: Brain-Computer Interfaces for AAC: Hybrid SSVEP + Eye-Tracking for Faster Selection Rates
items.abstract: Augmentative and alternative communication systems are essential for people with severe speech and motor impairments, yet many interfaces remain slow, effortful, and error-prone. This study evaluated a hybrid brain-computer interface that combines steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEP) with eye-tracking to improve selection speed, reliability, and usability. Participants completed symbol selection, short phrase construction, and correction tasks under three conditions: SSVEP-only, eye-tracking-only, and hybrid SSVEP plus eye-tracking. In the hybrid condition, gaze rapidly narrowed the likely target region, while SSVEP classification confirmed user intent. Outcomes included selection rate, accuracy, errors, correction time, communication throughput, workload, effort, trust, and preference. The hybrid interface achieved the strongest performance, with faster selection than SSVEP-only and better control than eye-tracking-only. It also reduced accidental selections and correction burden, particularly in dense layouts and longer tasks. Results further emphasized personalized gaze thresholds, SSVEP windows, and visual layouts for sustained, practical AAC use across diverse user needs.

items.title: BrainCodes: A Lightweight EEG Foundation Model over Discrete Neural Codes
items.abstract: Recent electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models increasingly emphasize model scale, potentially limiting their deployment on resource-constrained devices and in everyday environments. We argue that transferable EEG features can instead be learned with a compact architecture and introduce BrainCodes, a lightweight foundation model pretrained through self-supervised learning on more than 800 hours of recordings from over 1,000 participants. Our architecture combines a quantization-based neural tokenizer with a spatiotemporal encoder that supports arbitrary electrode configurations. The pretraining objective explicitly encourages representations that capture spatial connectivity through channel positional encoding, and sensitivity to narrowband neural oscillations through an auxiliary training objective. Our model matches or surpasses the state of the art across diverse neurophysiological monitoring tasks, including sleep staging, attention assessment, and cognitive load estimation. BrainCodes transfers effectively to low-resource wearable devices while using up to 97% fewer trainable parameters than comparable architectures. Beyond predictive accuracy, our evaluation framework characterizes the geometry and invariances of learned EEG representations across measurable spatial, temporal, and spectral signal properties.

items.title: Breaking the high-degree barrier in Lehmer's problem with a human-AI discovery loop
items.abstract: While artificial intelligence has made rapid progress in mathematical reasoning, many open problems depend on structure that is revealed only through large-scale computational exploration and analytical synthesis. One such example is Lehmer's problem from 1933. It asks whether the Mahler measure of an integer polynomial, which measures how far its roots stray from the unit circle, can be made arbitrarily small. Previously, constructing irreducible polynomials with integer coefficients and small Mahler measure has been carried out systematically only for even degrees $d \le 180$. At higher degrees, Boyd's analytical one-parameter family frequently factors, skipping nearly 50% of target degrees and leaving no general construction for arbitrary $d$. Here, we address the high-degree regime through a human-AI discovery loop, in which we extend the conversational prompting with a fast numerical pipeline, an exact symbolic verifier, and large-scale distributed search. The AI agent prototypes numerical and symbolic solvers locally, launches parallel searches across distributed clusters and works with the human researcher to extract and verify mathematical hypotheses. Through this interactive loop, we derive a five-parameter construction, which we call the Generalized Boyd algorithm. It eliminates degree-skipping and constructs irreducible polynomials with Mahler measure strictly below Boyd's limit point $α_1 \approx 1.255434$ for every target degree. Evaluated across all even degrees up to 2000, our approach improves upon six previously published values and holds 99.6% of all best known records. With this work we release the verified dataset of polynomials with minimal Mahler measure across all studied even degrees.

items.title: Bridging AI perceptions and insurance purchase intentions: the mediating role of perceived ease of use
items.abstract: Purpose The insurance industry is being transformed as artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping customer interactions, insurers' underwriting practices and service delivery. However, there is limited research or evidence on how customers' perceptions of AI-driven insurance services influence their purchase intentions. Taking inputs from technology acceptance model (TAM), this study investigates the relationship between customers' perceptions of AI-driven insurance services (CP-AI) and insurance purchase intentions (IPI) through the mediating role of the perceived ease of use (PEU). Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional design was used in the study to collect the responses from 490 insurance customers from India who were familiar with AI-enabled insurance services. As CP-AI cannot be directly measured, it was conceptualised as a second-order reflective construct consisting of four important dimensions, i.e. attitude towards AI, AI service experience, trust in AI services and technology readiness. The hypothesised relationships were tested using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). Findings The findings of the study highlights that the CP-AI have a significant positive impact on their purchase intentions. In addition, PEU partially mediates the relationship between CP-AI and their purchase intentions. Research limitations/implications The findings indicate that when customer perceptions are favourable, they are more effectively converted into IPI. In other words, if the AI-enabled insurance services are viewed as simple and effortless to use, the favourable customer perceptions are more likely to be converted into stronger IPI. These findings support the premise of the TAM that PEU is an important element linking technology perceptions to behavioural intentions, even in AI-enabled insurance service contexts. Practical implications The findings of the study provide practical insights for insurers to improve AI adoption among their customers by designing customer-friendly and easy-to-use AI-driven services, which will further improve customer acceptance and strengthen their purchase intentions. Originality/value This study extends research on AI-enabled insurance adoption by examining how customer perceptions influence purchase intentions through PEU. Its originality lies in conceptualising customer perceptions as a second-order reflective construct comprising attitude towards AI, AI service experience, trust in AI and technology readiness. Drawing on the TAM, the study demonstrates that perceived ease of use serves as an important mechanism linking favourable AI perceptions with purchase intentions. Based on responses from 490 Indian insurance customers, the study extends TAM to the AI-driven insurance context and offers practical insights for designing intuitive, customer-centric AI services.

items.title: Building and Maintaining Trust in AI Chatbots: Introducing Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF)
items.abstract: Social integration of AI requires public trust and appropriate governance. This paper introduces the Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF), designed to appraise accountability for Large Language Models and their applications, including AI chatbots. Drawing on Dahl’s (1998) notion of enlightened citizens, the framework comprises six interlinked dimensions: Information Readiness, Factual Correctness, Normative Alignment, Sourcing Practice, Transparency and Explainability, and Responsiveness and Adaptivity. Together, these dimensions link observable text outputs to intelligible standards, enabling systematic evaluation and accountable oversight. For scholars, developers and policymakers, GIRAAF provides a diagnostic heuristic and shared vocabulary for critical analysis of AI chatbot performance.

items.title: Business Ethics and Governance in Digital Transformation: Protecting Human Agency Through Inclusive Corporate Policies
items.abstract: Corporate digital governance often fails to mitigate the social impact of digitalization due to short-term profit optimization, triggering AI black box phenomena that marginalize digital workers' welfare. This study explores the integration of ethical dimensions into corporate governance frameworks to safeguard stakeholder rights. Employing a qualitative literature review approach (2019–2026), this research analyzes technology corporations' accountability regarding automated work systems. The findings reveal that current platform governance prioritizes financial gains over social equity, leading to algorithmic opacity and worker vulnerability in Indonesia. Consequently, this research concludes that algorithmic transparency must become an integral part of corporate compliance. The study recommends mandating boards of directors to implement periodic ethical audits on artificial intelligence systems to ensure business sustainability and distributive justice.

items.title: Cache Locally, Recompute Selectively for Streaming Video Understanding
items.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires video-LLMs to process incoming video continuously while answering user queries with low latency. Recent methods reduce query-time cost by prefilling frames into KV caches during idle time and reusing the cached KVs at query time. To bound per-frame computation over unbounded video streams, these methods restrict the context available during prefill. This creates a fundamental context mismatch: the restricted context may omit information needed to properly contextualize video tokens, yet, still contain information irrelevant to the eventual query, which is unknown during prefill. We propose FrameBlend, a simple yet effective plug-and-play method to address this mismatch through selective KV recomputation, without requiring any additional training. At query time, FrameBlend re-prefills selected video tokens using query-relevant context and replaces their cached KVs with recomputed ones. Crucially, this recomputation enables shorter attention windows during idle-time prefill, substantially reducing prefill cost while improving accuracy. Experiments across three SVU frameworks and five streaming and offline benchmarks demonstrate accuracy gains of up to 3.9 pp. On RVS-Ego, FrameBlend reduces per-frame prefill FLOPs by over 20% and total processing time by 14-59% for retrieval-based frameworks, including the cost of query-time recomputation. These results demonstrate that a simple change in how contextualization is distributed between idle time and query time can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for SVU.

items.title: Calibrated Uncertainty Propagation for Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Drought Early Warning Under Sparse Rain-Gauge Networks: A Computer Risk-Coverage Evaluation
items.abstract: Drought early warning systems that fuse satellite rainfall estimates with sparse rain-gauge networks must decide not only whether to issue an alert but also how much confidence to attach to it. The framework treats the classifier's predictive distribution as a calibrated object and evaluates it through the risk-coverage curve, which reports the selective error remaining after abstention at each coverage level. A propagation operator is defined that maps gauge-network density and satellite product uncertainty into the calibration of the predictive distribution, and a coverage guarantee is derived under an exchangeability assumption. The analysis is methodological: it specifies the estimator, the calibration diagnostic and the coverage bound, and it demonstrates how the risk-coverage curve changes as the propagation operator is tightened. The computed warming trend for the site is −0.1564 °C per decade, which the framework treats as a calibration-relevant drift term rather than as a drought signal. The contribution is a formal account of how uncertainty propagates from sparse gauges to alert confidence, and a decision rule that ties abstention to calibrated risk rather than to a fixed probability threshold.

items.title: Can LLMs Improve Their Own Harness? A Controlled Study on ARC-AGI-3
items.abstract: A generally intelligent system acquires new skills efficiently without requiring humans to redesign its software scaffold for every new task. Yet language models rarely act alone. A harness is a symbolic program that orchestrates calls to the model, handling perception, memory, tool use, recovery, and inference allocation on the model's behalf. ARC-AGI-3 is an interactive benchmark in which agents must explore unfamiliar environments, figure out their goals on the fly, and keep learning as they go. On it, human-steered systems already report ceiling scores across the public games, so we know effective designs exist. We ask whether frontier models can build and improve such a harness on their own. Through a fixed coding bootstrap, each model constructs a complete task harness, acts through that harness on five development games, and revises the entire codebase twice. Every version is evaluated on twenty games that never influence adaptation. We measure task performance with Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), which combines level completion with action efficiency relative to human baselines, and record dollar-denominated inference cost as a practical resource measure. Across 27 lineages, harness performance ranges from zero to near-ceiling scores. Two revisions raise mean held-out RHAE by only 2.80 points (95% interval [-1.44,7.35]). Development gains overstate held-out improvement, and reductions in inference cost can come at the expense of task performance. Human-steered systems demonstrate further headroom. These findings reveal a gap between autonomous harness construction and reliable adaptation under this two-revision protocol: even strong task performance does not ensure that subsequent revisions generalize or preserve existing capabilities.

items.title: Causal Estimation of Artificial Intelligence Diagnostic Delay Under Variable Radiology Reporting Queues: A Target-Trial Emulation of Healthcare Escalation Timing for Chest Radiograph Triage
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence triage of chest radiographs is often evaluated by discrimination and calibration, yet the clinically decisive quantity is the delay it introduces or removes from the escalation pathway. That delay is not a property of the model alone: it is produced jointly by model sensitivity, the queue discipline of the reporting service, and the timing rules that govern when a radiograph is escalated to a human reader. the present analysis formalises the escalation pathway as a target trial and derives the before-after-control-impact estimator appropriate to its emulation under staggered site-level adoption. Because no observational cohort is available, the design's operating characteristics are characterised analytically and by a replication-based evaluation under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64. Across 2000 replications per design cell and cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32, the analysis identifies the cluster count at which a 5 percentage-point reduction in time-to-escalation is detectable at 80% power as 54. The contribution is a design-theoretic account of what a causal claim about AI diagnostic delay would require, and a demonstration that queue variability, not model accuracy, is the binding constraint on the estimand's identifiability.

items.title: Causal Estimation of Artificial Intelligence Readmission Risk Under Variable Community Health Worker Visit Records: A Negative-Control Outcome Evaluation of Healthcare Resource Misallocation
items.abstract: Predictive models that flag patients for readmission risk are increasingly used to allocate post-discharge resources, but their training labels are drawn from community health worker (CHW) visit records that vary in completeness across clinics and payers. the present analysis treats that variation as a causal identification problem rather than a data-cleaning nuisance. It formalises the readmission-risk estimator as a function of both true clinical need and visit-record observability, and shows that the resulting misallocation is not a bias in the conventional sense but a stable equilibrium in which under-recorded patients are systematically under-served. A negative-control outcome design is proposed to detect and bound this misallocation: a placebo outcome that cannot be affected by the intervention but shares the same recording mechanism is used to estimate the recording-driven component of the risk score. The design is characterised analytically and evaluated through a replication-based power analysis under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64). Power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a design, not an estimate: a negative-control outcome framework that makes the recording mechanism visible in readmission-risk evaluation, together with the operating characteristics that determine whether such an evaluation is feasible in a given health system.

items.title: Certified Adversarial Transferability Bounds for Artificial Intelligence Cyclone Track Emulators Under Multi-Model Ensemble Disagreement: Attack Success Guarantees and Evacuation Order Safety
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence cyclone track emulators are increasingly used to generate evacuation triggers, yet their adversarial robustness is typically assessed only against the emulator that was attacked. The framework combines a Lipschitz continuity condition on the emulator mapping with a disagreement radius derived from ensemble spread, yielding a certified upper bound on the probability that a perturbation crafted for a source emulator succeeds against a target emulator. The bound is expressed as a function of the perturbation magnitude, the spectral norm of the emulator Jacobian, and the pairwise disagreement between ensemble members. A case study using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Lagos, Nigeria (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations) illustrates the calibration of the disagreement radius; the observed mean temperature was 26.414 °C and the warming trend was 0.1553 °C per decade. The framework yields an evacuation-order safety condition that translates the certified bound into a maximum permissible perturbation magnitude for a given false-alarm tolerance. The contribution is a formal, assumption-explicit guarantee that links adversarial transferability to ensemble disagreement and to the operational safety of evacuation decisions.

items.title: Certified Fairness Auditing for Artificial Intelligence Climate-Insurance Payout Models Under Covariate Shift: Disparity Bounds and Smallholder Compensation Equity
items.abstract: Climate-index insurance payout models increasingly rely on machine-learning predictors trained on historical weather and yield data, yet covariate shift between training and deployment distributions can silently widen compensation disparities between smallholder and commercial farms. The framework is operationalised on NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Accra, Ghana (2000–2023, 312 observations), where the estimated mean temperature is 26.521 °C and the warming trend is 0.1622 °C per decade, establishing a concrete shift regime against which audit thresholds can be calibrated. Formal results establish that the certified disparity bound decomposes into a shift-invariant base disparity plus a shift-amplified term controlled by the Wasserstein radius, and that the bound is tight for threshold payout rules. Auditing only marginal parity is insufficient under shift, because conditional payout gaps can grow while marginal gaps remain stable. The contribution is a certifiable audit protocol that converts covariate-shift assumptions into enforceable disparity bounds for smallholder compensation equity.

items.abstract: Neural climate emulators are increasingly used to produce seasonal forecasts, yet their reliability collapses when forced by radiative or land-surface conditions outside the training distribution. The framework combines a Mahalanobis-style score in a learned latent space with a conformal calibration layer, producing a certified threshold that controls the probability of silently accepting an OOD input. We derive high-probability bounds on the score gap between in-distribution and OOD regimes, and show that the certified threshold is achievable with a calibration sample whose size scales logarithmically in the confidence level. The framework is illustrated on a reanalysis-derived temperature series for Nairobi, Kenya (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 20.146 °C, warming trend 0.2477 °C per decade), where the emulator's latent score exhibits a clear separation between historical and perturbed forcing regimes. The certified detector attains a bounded false-negative rate under a range of computed forcing perturbations while preserving in-distribution coverage. The analysis clarifies when OOD certification is feasible for climate emulators and when it is not, and it identifies the calibration budget as the binding constraint on seasonal forecast safety.

items.abstract: Pest classifiers deployed on field-acquired images are exposed to adversarial perturbations that can flip a confident prediction while remaining visually inconspicuous to a human scout. The classifier is smoothed by adding isotropic Gaussian noise to the input and taking a majority vote over the induced distribution; the resulting certificate bounds the L2 radius within which no perturbation can change the predicted class. The analysis is a design and power study, not an observational one: the operating characteristics of the certification procedure are evaluated across a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, using 2000 replications per design cell over cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design attains 80% power at 5 percentage points with 52 clusters. The certified radius is a deployment parameter rather than a benchmark score, and that the intraclass correlation of field imagery governs how many independent field clusters a certification claim requires. The contribution is a formal certificate, a power-calibrated protocol for evaluating it, and a boundary condition: certification is informative only when the smoothing variance is matched to the perturbation budget the deployment actually faces.

items.title: Certified Shift-Aware Uncertainty Quantification for Artificial Intelligence Seasonal Precipitation Forecasts Under Volcanic Aerosol Injection: Coverage Bounds and Famine Early-Warning Trigger Reliability
items.abstract: Volcanic aerosol injection could alter seasonal precipitation patterns in ways that existing artificial intelligence (AI) forecast systems have never encountered, yet famine early-warning triggers built on those forecasts carry no formal reliability guarantee under such distributional shift. The framework combines a divergence-based shift detector, a distributionally robust conformal prediction layer, and a trigger reliability calculus that maps forecast intervals to famine early-warning activation probabilities. Formal results establish that the coverage gap under shift is bounded by the total variation distance between source and target distributions, that the trigger false-alarm rate is controlled at a user-specified level, and that the bound is tight in a minimax sense. The analysis is methodological and theoretical: no empirical forecast data are analysed, and the framework is presented as a certified design that would require validation against reanalysis and observational records before operational deployment. The contribution is a set of coverage and reliability guarantees that make the epistemic status of famine triggers explicit under a forcing scenario for which no historical training analogue exists.

items.title: Certified Temporal Fusion of Artificial Intelligence Climate Analytics for Crop Failure Early Warning Under Sparse Agricultural Sensors: Error Bounds and Famine Relief Targeting
items.abstract: Sparse agricultural sensor networks across sub-Saharan Africa leave crop-failure early-warning systems with too little ground observation to support reliable famine relief targeting. The framework treats sensor sparsity as a missing-data problem with a known observation operator and propagates climate-analytics uncertainty through a temporal Kalman-Buys filter whose gain is constrained by a certified risk envelope. Using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Accra, Ghana (2000-2023, 312 observations), the analysis establishes a mean temperature of 26.521 C and a warming trend of 0.1622 C per decade, which calibrates the climate-analytics prior. The derived bounds show that relief-targeting error scales with the square root of sensor density and with the Lipschitz constant of the crop-response function, yielding an explicit sensor-placement rule for a target misclassification rate. The contribution is a certified, assumption-explicit bridge between climate analytics and famine relief targeting that states the conditions under which early warning is trustworthy.

items.title: CertMoE: Robustness Certification for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs via Routing-Aware Smoothing
items.abstract: Provable robustness is a cornerstone of trustworthy machine learning, aiming to guarantee model predictions under adversarial perturbations. Existing certification frameworks, inspired by abstract interpretation or symbolic execution, typically assume a fixed computation graph, where input perturbations or variations affect only model outputs but not the underlying execution path. This assumption, however, is violated in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs), whose input-dependent routing induces discrete and dynamic execution paths. Crucially, this dynamic computation changes the certified object from a single fixed function to a composition of input-dependent sub-functions, leading to unreliable certification guarantees. This paper presents \textsc{CertMoE}, the first routing-aware robustness certification framework for MoE LLMs, which explicitly accounts for input-induced routing dynamics in certification. Specifically, we introduce a relaxed routing-containment criterion, which certifies that perturbed Top-$K$ routing is contained within a larger certified expert pool. Based on this guarantee, \textsc{CertMoE} then constructs the corresponding induced sub-network and certifies its prediction consistency. This hierarchical certification procedure yields a joint probabilistic guarantee over routing containment and sub-network robustness, providing sufficient conditions under which the original prediction remains invariant. Extensive experiments across recent MoE LLMs demonstrate that dynamic routing makes certificates issued by existing methods frequently violated, while \textsc{CertMoE} reduces the empirical violation rate with routing-aware guarantees, e.g., from more than $30\%$ to $0$, yielding certificates that more faithfully reflect the robustness of MoE models.

items.title: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis
items.abstract: Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent's reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. We first build \probe{}, a suite of 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions, and find a persistent gap between what agents can read and what they choose to use. Agents score as well from self-generated charts as from numeric output, yet plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Task slices show that charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification. We then propose \method{}, which distils two families of experience from conditioned trajectory rollouts. One family records how to select and verify analytical operations, and the other records when to invoke text, charts, or both. A trajectory judge scores outcomes and labels intermediate steps, and a validation gate admits only experience that improves held-out performance. On three held-out benchmarks with four LLM backbones, \method{} raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines, and backbones that never drew charts begin using them, all without touching model parameters.

items.title: ChatGPT as a Shopping Assistant: Effects of Perceived Ease of Use, Perceived Usefulness, Anthropomorphism, and Navigation on Satisfaction and Purchase Intention
items.abstract: In the context of ChatGPT as a shopping assistant in Indonesia, this research investigates the correlations between satisfaction and factors such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, ease of use, and navigation, as well as the link between satisfaction and buy intention. Using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research takes into account functional perceptions in addition to conversational AI's human-like and interaction-related traits. The data were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM) with AMOS from a quantitative, cross-sectional survey that was administered to 200 participants. The findings show that elements such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, and navigation are positively and substantially linked to satisfaction. There is a positive correlation between perceived ease of use and satisfaction, however the link is not statistically significant (β = 0.135, p = 0.063). Having a positive and substantial association with purchase intention (β = 0.537, p < 0.001) constitutes satisfaction. It turns out that four out of five possibilities are correct. According to the results, in this particular sample, features connected to interactions and practical utility are linked to satisfaction, although simplicity of use by itself does not show any statistical significance. Caution is required due to the study's cross-sectional methodology and conflicting model-fit results, but it does expand the applicability of TAM to conversational shopping help in Indonesia.

items.title: ChatGPT as a Supporting Medium for Islamic Religious Education: Strengthening Students’ Learning Experience and Academic Integrity
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, offers opportunities to enhance learning while raising concerns about academic integrity. This study examines the role of ChatGPT in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) and formulates strategies to preserve students’ academic integrity. Using a qualitative library research approach, it analyzes scientific articles, books, policy documents, and other credible sources on generative AI, IRE, learning autonomy, and academic integrity through content analysis and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that ChatGPT can improve access to learning resources, support independent learning, clarify complex concepts, and provide preliminary feedback. However, excessive reliance may encourage plagiarism, weaken critical thinking, reduce originality, and produce inaccurate information. Six complementary strategies are proposed: institutional policies, academic guidelines, cultivation of academic honesty, higher-order thinking tasks (C4–C6), authentic performance-based assessment, and contextual and problem-based learning. These strategies position ChatGPT as a supporting tool rather than a substitute for students’ intellectual processes, and its outputs must be critically verified against credible scholarly sources. The study concludes that the educational value of ChatGPT in IRE depends on sound pedagogical design and a strong ethical framework. Because the framework is a conceptual synthesis of the literature, it has not been empirically validated and should be tested in future research.

items.title: ChatGPT in the Classroom: An Exploration of First-Generation and Hispanic/Latino/a Student Perceptions
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines how first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a students enrolled in an introductory undergraduate psychology course perceived the influence of ChatGPT, a generative AI tool, on their academic skill development, learning experiences, and confidence. This study surveyed 88 students enrolled across four sections of an introductory undergraduate psychology course, with the goal of understanding student perceptions of ChatGPT. Of those surveyed, 67% identified as first-generation, 55% as Hispanic/Latino/a, and 41.9% as both first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a. Analyses suggested that first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a students reported more favorable perceptions of ChatGPT’s usefulness than their peers. While the study does not claim generalizability, its findings offer insight into how diverse students perceived AI tools in this educational setting. Interpretations are informed by the Digital Learning Ecosystem and decolonial pedagogy frameworks. Implications for instruction include opportunities for scaffolding AI use to support student agency, identity, and academic confidence in classroom environments.

items.title: Circuits of LLM Classifiers
items.abstract: Language models make it easy to build classifiers by simply prompting a model with the sample to classify. However, their predictions are neither deterministic nor uniformly reliable across samples. How can we combine predictions from different models to improve reliability? We view LLM classifiers as noisy measurement instruments of an underlying target label. Our goal is to maximize average classification accuracy at a given average query cost. To this end, we introduce circuits that organize LLM classifiers into an adaptive sequence of queries and decisions. We then characterize the optimal circuit, obtain the fundamental limits of achievable accuracy, and provide practical insights on realizing the optimal circuit. Across seven classification tasks spanning safety, health, political science, human preference, agent evaluation, decision-making and reasoning, our method improves the cost-accuracy frontier over routing and cascading baselines.

items.title: Clinical Computer Vision for Dengue Warning-Sign Recognition Under Variable Capillary Refill Assessment Skill: A Human-in-the-Loop Deferral Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Triage Safety
items.abstract: Dengue warning-sign recognition depends on capillary refill assessment, a bedside skill whose reliability varies widely among clinicians. Computer vision systems that estimate refill time from smartphone video could standardise triage, but their safety depends on how they interact with the variable skill of the humans who defer to them. The framework characterises triage safety through a deferral operating characteristic and derives the conditions under which machine deferral reduces, rather than redistributes, triage error. A design-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 percent power. The framework proposes that deferral safety is governed not by model accuracy alone but by the covariance between model and clinician errors, and that this covariance is itself a function of clinician skill. The contribution is a formal account of when human-in-the-loop deferral improves triage safety for dengue warning-sign recognition under variable capillary refill assessment skill.

items.title: Clinical Computer Vision for Sickle Cell Retinopathy Screening Under Variable Fundus Camera Resolution: A Super-Resolution Domain-Adaptation Evaluation of Referral Grading Safety
items.abstract: Sickle cell retinopathy screening in African primary care is constrained by fundus cameras of unequal resolution, and the safety of artificial-intelligence referral grading under that heterogeneity has not been characterised. The framework treats the referral decision as a thresholded function of a latent retinopathy severity score, decomposes the resolution-induced distribution shift into a recoverable component and an irreducible information-loss component, and derives a bound on the change in referral sensitivity under adaptation. A before-after-control-impact design with a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64) was used to characterise the operating characteristics of the evaluation design across 2000 replications per design cell, with cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design requires 54 clusters to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The framework proposes that adaptation safety should be reported as a resolution-stratified sensitivity profile rather than a single aggregate metric, and identifies the conditions under which super-resolution adaptation preserves or degrades referral safety. The contribution is a design-level and decision-level formalisation that makes resolution heterogeneity an explicit object of evaluation rather than an uncontrolled nuisance.

items.title: Closed-loop EEG feedback pacing alters task load during digital learning
items.abstract: Abstract Digital learning systems rarely adapt to momentary cognitive state, creating risk of underload or overload. The current study testes whether EEG-based closed-loop pacing can regulate task load dynamics during a digital constellation-learning task. Fifty-one participants were randomly assigned to adaptive, reward, or control conditions. In the adaptive condition, a task loas index derived from frontal theta and parietal alpha adjusted feedback duration between 3 and 8 s; fixed 5s feedback was used in reward and control conditions, with reward participants receiving performance-contingent draw entries. Accuracy increased across blocks in all groups, with no significant group or group-by-block effect. In contrast, EEG indices showed group-specific trajectories: task load decreased over time in the adaptive condition, and frontal theta and parietal alpha showed significant group-by-block interactions. The adaptive condition also showed reduced ate-session feedback duration, while reward participants reported higher satisfaction. intrinsic motivation did not moderate group effects, although perceived competence predicated final-block performance and interest and effort predicted engagement. These findings suggest that EEG-based feedback pacing can regulate neurophysiological task load dynamics despite lack of immediate accuracy gains under the present task constraints. The results support neuroadaptive scaffolding as a state-regulation mechanism for digital learning.

items.title: CloudIR-Bench: A Benchmark for Root Cause Analysis and Mitigation of Cloud Incidents
items.abstract: Root cause analysis (RCA) and mitigation prediction are essential for incident management, enabling the identification of underlying causes of failures and ensuring the reliability of complex cloud-based systems. With rising incident volume and system complexity, incident reports have become a valuable resource for these tasks. Recent studies have shown promising results using Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict root causes and mitigation actions from textual descriptions in incident reports. Despite these advances, further progress is hindered by the lack of publicly available datasets; existing work relies on private data, which limits transparency, reproducibility, and generalization. To address this gap, we introduce CloudIR-Bench, the first publicly available benchmark providing a dataset and evaluation framework for incident report-based RCA and mitigation prediction. Curated from incident reports across five leading cloud-based systems, CloudIR-Bench captures a diverse range of real-world production scenarios representing authentic failures and engineers' reasoning. We also release an open-source evaluation framework that includes eight recent LLM-based approaches. Our comprehensive evaluation includes zero-shot and in-context learning experiments, along with a qualitative analysis to identify where and why LLMs fail. Benchmarking results reveal the capabilities and limitations of existing LLMs in this domain. The benchmark, including the dataset, framework and supplementary materials, is available at https://github.com/hoangtnm/CloudIR-Bench.
